title: Human-Centered Generative AI Auditing Platform
oneLiner: An open-source platform for studies that mix surveys, live chatbot conversations, and guided auditing.
teaser: An open-source platform for studies that combine surveys, live chatbot conversations, and guided auditing tasks. I build the annotation tools, the study flows, and the export pipeline that turns conversations into analyzable data.
summary: An open-source platform for studies that combine surveys, live chatbot conversations, and guided auditing tasks. I design and build the system, including its annotation tools, study flows, and structured data export.
problem: Benchmarks measure what a model does on fixed inputs. They don't tell you what a person sitting in front of the model actually notices or questions. Getting that kind of evidence takes real software — consent flows, tutorials, a chat interface, annotation tools, a data pipeline — and most research teams rebuild all of it for every study.
role: I design and build the platform, and I use it to run my own auditing studies.
built: Study flows that combine surveys, live chatbot conversations, and guided auditing tasks
Turn-level highlighting and annotation of model responses
Likert-scale and free-text responses tied to specific conversation turns
Tutorial gating so participants practice the auditing task before the main study
Structured data storage, export, and study replay
Study content kept separate from system logic, so a new study is a configuration, not a rewrite
scale: Used in a study with 254 participants and 551 conversations

title: How People Audit and Trust Generative AI
oneLiner: We asked 254 people to hunt for problems in AI chatbots. Many came away trusting the chatbot more.
teaser: What do everyday users actually catch when you ask them to find problems in a chatbot? In 551 conversations, many participants missed the issues the study was designed to surface — and probing often made them more trusting, not less.
pullQuote: Hunting for problems usually left participants trusting the chatbot more — even when the hunt turned up little.
summary: We asked 254 U.S. participants to probe chatbots for problematic and unfair behavior — 551 conversations, run through an audit interface I built. Many missed issues the study was designed to surface, and the exercise often left them more trusting of the model.
problem: Product teams and regulators sometimes treat “let users try the model” as a check on AI systems. We tested what that check actually produces: what everyday users catch, what they miss, and what the exercise does to their trust.
whyItMatters: If probing leaves people more confident without making them better at finding problems, user testing can manufacture trust rather than measure it. And since participants who started out more trusting flagged fewer problems, the people most inclined to rely on a model are the least likely to catch its failures.
role: I led the interactive study and designed and deployed the chat, survey, and annotation system it ran on. Study design and analysis were joint work with a multi-institution team.
findings: Participants often failed to surface problems the study was designed to let them find.
Probing frequently increased trust in the chatbot, even when it was limited or unsuccessful.
Participants who began with higher trust flagged fewer problems.

A companion survey of 123 U.S. chatbot users found three distinct groups — Hesitant Skeptics, Cautious Trusters, and Confident Adopters — with usage frequency, not demographics, the strongest predictor of trust.
A review of 130 AI user studies found most rely on unvalidated rating scales, which is part of why we argue for validated instruments.
status: Published at FAccT 2026, SOUPS 2025, and ConPro 2025
collaborators: With co-authors at The George Washington University and partner universities.

title: How Privacy Disclosures Are Created, Maintained, and Understood
oneLiner: A multi-year study of Apple's privacy-label ecosystem, from large-scale measurement to developer surveys and interviews.
summary: Apple's privacy labels are intended to provide a concise account of an app's data practices. Across this research program, we track how labels are adopted and updated, compare them with apps' privacy policies, and study how developers interpret and maintain these disclosures.
problem: Privacy labels can only help users when they remain accurate as apps and their third-party dependencies change. Developers may be asked to report practices they do not fully control or understand, while disclosure tools remain disconnected from ordinary development workflows.
whyItMatters: Our findings show that disclosure failures are not explained only by deliberate deception. Ambiguous terminology, third-party SDKs, fragmented organizational responsibility, and limited maintenance support can allow labels to remain unchanged even when an app evolves.
role: My work in this research line spans longitudinal measurement, privacy-policy comparison, and developer-focused mixed-methods research.

title: Reflecting on AI Interaction Histories
oneLiner: A dashboard study of what people disclose to chatbots over months of use — and whether seeing it all changes anything.
summary: People tell chatbots things one conversation at a time, but providers keep the whole history. In this study, participants see their own history in a dashboard I am building — selected past conversations, resurfaced with reflection prompts — so we can measure what they notice about their disclosures and whether they change how they manage their data.
problem: A single conversation can feel disposable. A year of them can reveal health worries, finances, and relationships — and support inferences across conversations that no single exchange shows. Most people never look back at what they have shared.
role: I designed the study and I am building the dashboard and data-collection tooling.
built: A consent-based mechanism for collecting participants' own AI interaction histories
A participant-facing dashboard that resurfaces selected past conversations
Guided reflection prompts about sensitive disclosures and cross-conversation inference
Pre- and post-intervention measures of disclosure awareness, perceived privacy risk, perceived benefits, and intentions to review, delete, or manage stored histories
status: IRB approved · data collection in progress
statusNote: Results will be reported when data collection is complete.

title: AI in the Workplace: Adoption, Trust, and Governance
oneLiner: Interviews with employees and AI practitioners about what work goes to AI, who checks its output, and what employers do about it.
summary: Semi-structured interviews with employees and AI practitioners about how AI actually enters a workplace: which tasks it takes on, why people adopt or avoid it, how they check its output, and what their organizations do about any of it.
problem: Standards and governance frameworks address organizations, but adoption happens one person at a time. Governance that works in practice has to start from what employees actually do: the judgment calls, the double-checking, the workarounds.
questions: What tasks do employees hand to AI, and what does that change about their work?
Why do people adopt AI tools — or deliberately avoid them?
How do employees decide when AI use is appropriate, and how do they verify output?
What support and oversight do organizations actually provide?
How do practitioners run human-centered evaluations inside real organizations, and what evidence changes product and governance decisions?
role: I conduct interviews and qualitative analysis in a collaboration with NIST researchers.
collaborators: With researchers at the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST).
